subject.name: Ultranationalism
subject.description: An exclusionary political tradition placing national unity, sovereignty and power above competing loyalties and individual claims. This broad profile covers its statist forms across countries; economic programmes, religious foundations and ideas about ancestry vary between movements.
subject.period: Comparative modern tradition, late nineteenth century onward; research through 2026-10-07
subject.scope: A broad comparative assessment of statist, exclusionary ultranationalism rather than ordinary patriotism or all nationalism. It includes emperor-centred, secular and religious forms without requiring a Japanese emperor, a particular faith, biological racism, fascist national rebirth, or one economic model. Stateless fringe variants are outside this institutional scope. Every exact questionnaire response is an educated assumption: this family has no common 240-question manifesto. Economic, biomedical, religious and causal-trait responses have especially limited generalisability.
subject.phrase: A society united around its national identity, with public institutions, economic life and civic duties serving the nation’s sovereignty, strength and continuity above competing loyalties.

sources.title: Roger Griffin: Staging the Nation’s Rebirth
sources.publisher: Library of Social Science / Roger Griffin

sources.title: Nationalism: liberal, conservative and exclusionary distinctions
Japan’s Holy War: publisher synopsis of Walter Skya’s study

retrievalNotes: Read the linked definition, Griffin comparative essay, Stanford nationalism entry, USHMM fascism overview, Duke publisher synopsis (not the whole book), and Columbia primary-source selection page. Britannica and one Cambridge book URL failed and are not cited as read sources. Fascism is used as a related subtype, not an equation of all ultranationalism with fascism. No neighbour answer file was used to construct these responses.

axes.brief: National unity and decisive leadership are favoured over competitive constraints in the illiberal statist scope. Public mobilisation or plebiscites do not establish direct citizen control.
axes.counterEvidence: Ultranationalist movements can contest elections and retain parliamentary shells; no universal military rule or single institutional blueprint follows. Ordinary nationalism can be democratic and is excluded from this anti-pluralist scope. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Order, discipline and protection of the national community take priority over autonomous dissent. Narrow security or health measures are assessed on their own terms, not equated with autocracy.
axes.counterEvidence: Paramilitary mobilisation can support arms for loyalists, and restrictions can target outsiders selectively. No source establishes one universal vaccination, privacy or hatred-law programme. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: A predominant national identity and common public culture are central to this exclusionary scope. Cultural membership need not be defined solely by inherited race.
axes.counterEvidence: Some movements recognise native minorities or private customs they deem compatible with national unity. Recognition is not necessarily equal accommodation of migrant cultures. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Entry and membership are filtered through national continuity and exclusionary belonging, rather than a general right of settlement. Immigration is assessed separately from cultural assimilation.
axes.counterEvidence: Coethnic return, strategic labour recruitment and family reunification may receive exceptions. Restriction does not imply identical limits for every migrant or opposition to all asylum. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National power and willingness to use force support military capacity. Expansionist and defensive branches differ; not every nationalist is militarist.
axes.counterEvidence: Tactical negotiation and avoiding costly defeat can serve national strength. Autonomous weapons and gender-specific service are modern or programme-specific extrapolations. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National supremacy in law and policy is the defining commitment. Cooperation can be instrumental without transferring final authority.
axes.counterEvidence: Alliances, negotiated commerce and joint projects can further national power. Their existence is not evidence for supranational authority. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Ownership is instrumental to national strength. A mixed economy with domestic private enterprise and public strategic assets is the most likely interpretation of this broad statist scope.
axes.counterEvidence: Nationalisation, corporatism and pro-business variants differ. Command over firms is not ownership; no comprehensive socialist ownership requirement is inferred. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Economic sovereignty and domestic capacity favour protection where external dependence could constrain the nation. Useful trade remains possible.
axes.counterEvidence: Not all ultranationalist movements advocate autarky; export access and imports of needed technology can serve national strength. Product-tax design is distinct from tariffs. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National goals can direct investment and strategic production while ordinary markets persist. This is not a claim of complete central planning.
axes.counterEvidence: Nationalist pro-market and corporatist programmes differ. Security control, ownership, everyday price-setting and redistribution must not be collapsed into one economic score. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National solidarity can support member welfare, but income equalisation is not the central goal. Hierarchical and solidarist strands coexist; welfare is not inferred from immigration restriction.
axes.counterEvidence: Some ultranationalist programmes advocate extensive social benefits or land reform, others protect property and hierarchy. Neither a universal tax schedule nor equalisation doctrine is established. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National authority is primary. Religious and secular ultranationalisms exist, so no particular faith is required; common national ceremonies and heritage may still receive official recognition.
axes.counterEvidence: Shinto emperor doctrine is a religious branch, not the template for every country. Political sacralisation of the nation is not automatically clerical government or religious family law. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: National continuity, inherited public culture and disciplined family life favour traditional norms, while national renewal can overturn older political institutions.
axes.counterEvidence: Griffin’s revolutionary fascist branch is not simply restorationist. A general preference for national continuity does not prove a uniform programme on sexuality or abortion. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Technology and infrastructure can increase national capability. Land, health and national heritage can also warrant protection; no uniform biomedical risk doctrine follows.
axes.counterEvidence: Comparative research includes both technological and agrarian strands. Modern AI, cultivated meat, implants and gene editing are disclosed analogies, not documented common programmes. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: An integrated national authority is likely preferred where regions could obstruct common national purposes. Local administration can still implement the programme.
axes.counterEvidence: National self-determination against foreign rule differs from a right of internal secession. Local heritage and administrative efficiency can justify delegated decisions. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.

axes.brief: Nation-building through education, social discipline and shared experience supports cultural explanations for learned habits. Ethnic belonging is not automatically biological causal determinism.
axes.counterEvidence: Biological-racist branches exist, but comparative research explicitly distinguishes cultural, historical and ethnic membership from necessary biological racism. Trait-specific answers and response strengths remain weakly evidenced. Checked the linked comparative and national-identity research for opposing interpretations; no exact shared response to these 16 statements was found.
